dataflow.outcome: recoverable local archive integrity and availability failure for that object hash
dataflow.sink: published KCS tree, commit, and refs naming a corrupt raw object slot
dataflow.summary: preseeded occupied CAS slot -> `write_raw()` expected hash -> `atomic_write()` existing-path success -> working tree raw hash -> tree/commit/ref publication -> later read-time corruption error

impact.why: The primitive causes local archive integrity and availability loss for matching objects, but read-time verification prevents silent return of wrong bytes.

likelihood.why: The adopted/shared-state boundary is in scope, but exploitation needs exact-slot poisoning and an operator snapshot of matching content.

limitations: Private live-store arbitrary same-user tampering is out of scope.
Read-time digest verification detects wrong regular-file contents.
The corrupt slot can be manually repaired or quarantined.

reachability.entrypoint: adopted, copied, synced, shared, or preseeded `.kcs` store
reachability.outcome: future reads of the published object fail as corrupt, and future legitimate writes continue to accept the occupied slot as success
preconditions: The operator adopts lower-trust persisted KCS state.
The occupied object path exactly matches content the operator later snapshots.
The corrupt slot remains present when `atomic_write()` runs.
reachability.summary: The attacker must supply or influence adopted store state, know or select the content hash, and rely on the operator snapshotting content that maps to the poisoned slot.

attackPath.summary: A lower-trust archive-state contributor supplies a copied, shared, synced, or preseeded store containing a corrupt entry at the exact raw CAS path for content the operator later snapshots. KCS treats the occupied slot as a successful write, publishes history that names the expected hash, and later reports corruption when the object is read.

codeEvidence.explanation: `write_raw()` derives the authoritative object hash from the file bytes and then asks the shared writer to store those same bytes at the hash-derived path.
codeEvidence.label: Raw writes compute the expected CAS identity before storage

codeEvidence.explanation: A contributor who supplies or predicts the bytes can compute the exact raw object slot before the operator adopts the store.
codeEvidence.label: Hash fanout path is deterministic

codeEvidence.explanation: `atomic_write()` only checks whether the path exists. It does not verify the filesystem type, compare existing bytes with `bytes`, or reject an occupied corrupt slot before returning success.
codeEvidence.label: Existing destination is accepted without verification

codeEvidence.explanation: When `write_raw()` returns success, the working tree carries the expected hash forward even if the durable raw slot was not actually repaired or verified.
codeEvidence.label: Snapshot records the returned raw hash in the tree

codeEvidence.explanation: The accepted raw hash becomes part of the tree object that `snapshot_with_type()` is about to publish.
codeEvidence.label: Snapshot can publish history after the accepted write

codeEvidence.explanation: After the tree and commit writes succeed, refs can advance to history that points at the corrupt raw slot through the recorded tree entry.
codeEvidence.label: Refs advance to the commit that names the tree

codeEvidence.explanation: Later reads reject a hash mismatch, which prevents silent return of wrong bytes but leaves publication and future write repair blocked until the corrupt slot is manually removed or quarantined.
codeEvidence.label: Read path detects but does not repair corrupt objects

regressionTests: Preseed a raw CAS path with wrong bytes, snapshot matching content, and assert the write fails or quarantines before refs advance.
Preseed a raw CAS path with the exact expected bytes and assert idempotent success.
Preseed a CAS path with a directory, symlink, or other non-regular entry and assert failure.
Repeat occupied-slot checks for tree and commit object writes because they share `atomic_write()`.
remediation.summary: Before returning success for an existing destination, verify that it is a regular file and that its bytes match the bytes being written; reject or quarantine mismatches atomically so legitimate writes can recover.

rootCause.summary: The violated invariant is that an existing CAS destination is idempotent only if it is the exact regular object being written. `atomic_write()` returns success solely because the path exists, so a preseeded corrupt slot prevents both repair and failure while the snapshot path carries the expected hash into published tree and commit state.

summary: The KCS CAS writer treats any pre-existing object destination as a successful write without verifying that the occupied slot is a regular file containing the expected bytes. A lower-trust copied, shared, synced, or preseeded .kcs store can therefore contain a corrupt raw object at the exact fanout path for content the operator later snapshots; KCS reports the write as successful, publishes tree and commit state naming the expected hash, and only detects corruption on later reads.
title: CAS write accepts a pre-existing corrupt destination as success

assertions: A pre-existing regular file with wrong bytes at the exact fanout path is accepted as a successful write.
Snapshot can carry the expected hash into tree and commit publication even when the durable raw slot remains corrupt.
Read-time digest verification detects corruption but does not repair or unblock future writes to the occupied slot.
limitations: No end-to-end adopted-store runtime was recorded in the saved validation.
The PoC is local and synthetic; it does not touch a real operator store or any external system.
The prevalence of copied, synced, or preseeded lower-trust KCS stores is deployment-dependent.
validation.method: saved static source trace plus local/offline synthetic PoC
validation.summary: The saved validation confirms that all raw, tree, and commit writes reach `atomic_write()` and that the existing-destination branch returns success without checking type, bytes, or digest. The included PoC models the raw-object case with synthetic bytes and shows the corrupt slot remains occupied until a fixed check rejects it.
